plate.subject: Parim's towers above the Great Lake in sunlight

paragraphs.text: Elzon’s death ended the Third Age. The Great Necromancer had ruled Aenor for many generations, although the elves of the Magical Lands never submitted to him and men never ceased to resist. The good king who took the restored throne inherited ruined roads, cursed fields, divided provinces and a people who could scarcely remember independence.

sources.section: Prologue: the peace that followed Elzon

paragraphs.text: The scholars reckon the years of this age from the death of Elzon and the crowning of the first restored king, and they write them 4A. The first year of the restored monarchy is 4A 1, and in 4A 1748 the age is more than seventeen centuries old.

Aoaz keeps twelve months, and each honours and is named after one of the twelve main New Gods, who answer the twelve needs of mortals. The year opens with the month of Glernaen, the mightiest of the twelve, and the third month, Lumae, opens the spring. The lesser New Gods have no month, and the cult of the Deliverer keeps a feast of its own rather than a month.
paragraphs.note: The twelve months honouring the twelve main New Gods and the Deliverer’s feast are established; the month names Glernaen and Lumae and the spring falling from the third month come from the calendar decision K28 and the proposed seasons table.

paragraphs.text: For more than a thousand years the Middle Kingdom grew. Cities spread around the Great Lake and its ports expanded. Teachers, physicians and builders found patrons, and schools and libraries stood in places that plague had once ravaged. Trade grew with the North Lands, the West Lands, the islands, the Magical Lands and the eastern states. Dangerous borders remained, but the great invasions of orcs and goblins had ceased, and Aenor became as formidable as it had ever been.

sources.section: Prologue: the peace that followed Elzon

paragraphs.text: The histories agree that the peace was real. Aoaz knew more than a thousand years of genuine peace, plenty, learning and medicine under strong laws and courts, and the kingdoms that lived through it remember it as the longest good time the world has known.

sources.section: Prologue: the peace that followed Elzon

paragraphs.text: The scholars divide the age into the Restoration, which lasted until the First Concord Council of 4A 212; the Long Peace, which ended with the Thousand-Year Jubilee of 4A 1000; the Blessed Centuries that followed; and the reign of the Golden King, who was crowned in 4A 1729.

plate.subject: a coronation at Parim before rebuilt walls

paragraphs.text: In 4A 1, after Elzon’s death, Harion of Selen was crowned at Parim. He came of a lesser branch of Aen’s royal line and had earned his place through many years of resistance and organising against the occupation, so that his right rested on both descent and service. He was a good king, and he brought peace through rebuilding, law, fair grain stores, sensible defence and patient dealing with his neighbours.
paragraphs.note: A good king restoring a strong Aenor is established; the name Harion of Selen, his descent, his years of resistance and the date are proposed.

paragraphs.text: Harion did not make the Fourth Age’s prosperity alone. The cures, irrigation works, crop rotations, craft of fortification, clean wells and drains, and stores against famine worked out in the Second Age gave the new kingdom practical ways to rebuild, and Varner’s work against the curses of the dead made the old grave-fields fit to live in again.

sources.section: Prologue: the peace that followed Elzon

paragraphs.text: In the same first year the people acclaimed the Deliverer, who was honoured for saving Aenor at Elzon’s fall, under the name Aurevan. Harion welcomed the relief houses of the Deliverer’s followers because they plainly helped the people, and he gave them a place in the new kingdom.
paragraphs.note: The Deliverer’s public acclaim after Elzon’s fall is established; the name Aurevan, the year and Harion’s welcome of the relief houses are proposed.

paragraphs.text: Between 4A 40 and 4A 120 the roads, canals and Great Lake ports were rebuilt, and the medicine and farming of the Second Age returned to every province. From 4A 150 Aenoran merchants went back to the West Lands for the first time since the wars of the First Age. The western lords took the trade gladly, but they did not accept the old Aenoran claims.

Harion did not reign for the whole age. Successive kings and royal generations followed him on the throne of Parim, and the histories count the Restoration as the work of his house as much as his own. By the scholars’ reckoning it ended with the First Concord Council of 4A 212.

In 4A 3 the Charters of Parim bound the surviving dominions of the Middle Lands to the crown as self-governing members of a common defence. Each dominion kept its own lords and laws. The Charters are the root of the Middle Kingdom Concord, and Selen, Kilinti, Kingson, Konori, Hunhun and the rest still hold their lands under them.
Hirolon, the sovereign kingdom of the giants, stayed outside the Charters. It treats with the crown of Parim as one realm with another and has never been a dominion of Aenor.

Not every land of the Middle Lands came under them. The Cursed Lands and the Bloody Forest rejected the crown and reject it still. Within the Charters the lawyers of Parim do not agree whether a chartered dominion is a part of the kingdom or a realm allied to it, and they have argued the point for centuries.
paragraphs.note: The Cursed Lands and the Bloody Forest resisting the crown and the open constitutional status of the dominions are established; their link to the Charters is proposed.

sources.section: The Middle Lands: Aenor and the Concord

plate.subject: ploughmen in old grave-fields under a wizard's lantern

paragraphs.text: Varner is a wise wizard of the Magical Lands, a Lesser Spirit in the form of an old man. Through the long Third Age he helped the elves and the human resistance withstand Elzon’s necromancy, and he knew how to undo the curse that bound Elzon’s risen dead. A small purple servant of unknown origin, Golbran, goes with him.

Between 4A 4 and 4A 60 Varner’s Unbinding lifted the curse from the old grave-fields. Ploughmen went back to land that had been left to the dead for generations, and the restored kingdom could feed itself from fields that had been lost since the occupation.
paragraphs.note: Varner’s work making the old grave-fields habitable is established; the name of the Unbinding and its dates are proposed.

sources.section: Prologue: the peace that followed Elzon

paragraphs.text: When the work was done, the Lantern Chain, the network of couriers, hidden refuges and ward-keepers that Varner and Golbran had built in the Third Age, had no more need of secrecy. It dissolved into the village healers and wardens of the Middle Lands, who carried its remedies and its wards into the new kingdom.

Varner’s wisdom has been heeded for centuries since, although his order is still that of a Lesser Spirit. He is one practitioner among many traditions of magic, and Bastian, a living human wizard famous in the Middle Lands, is his contemporary.

The Great Wall of Aenor is no work of masons. It is an enormous natural range of mountains between the Middle Lands and the Magical Lands, held by dwarves, and its passes, valleys and snowlines decide every road between the two lands. Elzon’s Order kept watch-posts in its passes against the Magical Lands, which it never conquered.
paragraphs.note: The Great Wall as a natural range held by dwarves is established; the watch-posts of Elzon’s Order are proposed.

paragraphs.text: In 4A 96 Harion’s grandson and the elven realms made the Accord of the Passes, which the pass folk call the Wall Accord. They agreed to keep a few passes guarded rather than open every road. The elves wanted their old separation, and the kings wanted customs posts on the pass roads and a watch against the dragons of the east. A few passes still carry the Accord’s watchtowers and customs posts.

sources.section: The Middle Lands: Aenor and the Concord

paragraphs.text: The Wall Accord is broken. A pass of the Great Wall changed hands by force of arms in war, and with it fell the old promise that the passes would be kept and not fought over.

plate.subject: a hall of dominion banners; university cloisters

paragraphs.text: In 4A 212 the dominions and the crown met in Parim at the First Concord Council. They agreed on a common army in war and free roads in peace, and from that day the members of the Charters spoke of themselves as one Concord. The scholars end the Restoration with this council and begin the Long Peace.
In 4A 340 the universities of Parim and Selen were founded, and physicians of the Houses of the First Light taught in both. Their scholars keep the histories from which this Chronicle is drawn.

In 4A 1748 the Concord counts twenty-six chartered dominions under the crown of Parim, and it still answers to the bargain of 4A 212: one army when the kingdom is at war, and open roads when it is not.
paragraphs.note: The twenty-six dominions are the working table; the bargain of 4A 212 is proposed.

sources.section: The Middle Lands: Aenor and the Concord

entries.title: The Union of the Leren Crowns
entries.subtitle: Fourth Age · Union

paragraphs.text: In 4A 411 the Leren crowns united. Lerendor and Lerendor’s North married their royal houses and became one kingdom, which has been the strongest power of the North Lands ever since.

The united crown rules from Sonargur and leads the Leren Compact with Eekedor. Its kings are proud, its fleets guard the strait, and Lerendor and Aenor have been rivals for as long as both have been strong. The smaller crowns of the North Lands, among them Tolvael, Molot, R’en and Mina, look to Lerendor or to Parim as it suits them.
paragraphs.note: Lerendor’s seat, the Leren Compact and the rivalry with Aenor are the working table; the fleets and the smaller crowns’ loyalties are proposed.

paragraphs.text: Between 4A 600 and 4A 780 the great caravan roads of the East Lands opened. Noris and Stabilo grew rich on them and began a rivalry that never fully ended. The East Lands became the richest region of Aoaz and remain the most divided, for Alerhia, Miaed, Erco and Plutondo are great kingdoms in their own right.

sources.section: The East Lands and the South Lands

paragraphs.text: Noris rules from Furvior and holds the Noris Treaty with Gondolin, and Stabilo rules from Postondoroth and holds the Stabilo Pact with Drak. The two compete for the southern trade roads, and each watches the other more closely than any enemy.

sources.section: The East Lands and the South Lands

paragraphs.text: In 4A 702 the Triton islanders charted the sea that their island arcs enclose and sold their charts to every crown. Captains still say that the best soundings in Aoaz are the Pupor charts. Adel, Pollos, Raerby, Nondondor and thirty island lordships live by fishing, by charting and, when the charts do not sell, by piracy.

sources.section: Triton's Islands and the Islands of the South

paragraphs.text: In 4A 850 Coldor’s kings brought the frozen interior of the Cold Lands under one crown. Isengard refused and has been Coldor’s enduring rival ever since. Coldor rules from Fandanar over the interior and the western ports and leads the Northern Accord with Horidor.

plate.subject: a feast in Parim under sun-marked temple banners

paragraphs.text: In 4A 1000 Parim celebrated a thousand years of peace. Envoys came from every region of Aoaz to see it, and Aurevan’s temples blessed the crown in front of them while the city feasted in its streets and on the shores of the Great Lake.

Later historians date the end of the high peace to the year of the Jubilee, although the peace itself went on for seven centuries more. The scholars of Parim and Selen still argue about what changed after it, and the Jubilee is where most of them begin the Blessed Centuries.

sources.section: III. The Kingdom Behind the Throne, 4A 1000 to 4A 1729

paragraphs.text: The centuries after the Jubilee are remembered as the Blessed Centuries. Kings reigned in Parim in peace, one after another, and few of them are remembered for anything else. Priests of Aurevan taught the princes, the Houses of the First Light kept the kingdom’s grain, hospitals and rolls, and a royal councillor who stood well with the temples was thought the mark of a wise court.
paragraphs.note: Priests educating princes and the Houses keeping the records are established; the name Aurevan and the Houses’ name are proposed.

sources.section: Prologue: the peace that followed Elzon
III. The Kingdom Behind the Throne, 4A 1000 to 4A 1729

paragraphs.text: Aurevan was praised as a New God of Deliverance, Protection and Renewal, and his blessings could be real. He could heal, shield, grant wealth and turn aside disaster. Most of the men who advised the kings counted service to the Deliverer an honourable service to their country.

sources.section: Prologue: the peace that followed Elzon

paragraphs.text: Beyond the Great Lake the centuries were less quiet. Orc warlords united the inner Dark Lands as Goldoroth, a temple-state of the Deliverer grew in the Zilin Hills, Volgan’s strength returned in the south, and the West Lands fell into the Gunwaith–Girdon wars. None of it reached Parim, where the kings went on reigning in peace.

sources.section: III. The Kingdom Behind the Throne, 4A 1000 to 4A 1729

paragraphs.text: The Blessed Centuries were the age of the Kingdom Behind the Throne. About 4A 1100 Afrit’s Hidden Council took its lasting form, with seats for royal administration, worship, foreign agents and the recovery of artifacts, and from 4A 1140 successive kings reigned while the Council governed. About 4A 1300 its eastern branch began to court the East Lands and South Lands as a reserve seat of power.
paragraphs.note: Afrit’s council ruling Aenor through its kings is established; the dates and the four seats are proposed.

sources.section: III. The Kingdom Behind the Throne, 4A 1000 to 4A 1729

paragraphs.text: The change was hard to see from one reign to the next. By the middle centuries Afrit’s people could help appoint councillors, decide which noble houses prospered, direct spies and govern without signing a single royal decree. Aenor’s kings wore the crown, but its true ruler was often elsewhere, which is why the kingdom stayed rich while its independence was slowly lost.

sources.section: Prologue: the peace that followed Elzon

plate.subject: orc war-banners over a Dark Lands hold

paragraphs.text: About 4A 1450 orc warlords united the inner Dark Lands as Goldoroth, and its wars with the human kingdom of Dondor began. Goldoroth rules from Cocanoor and wants the whole region. Dondor rules from Notbuton and leads the Dark Sea Accord with Belonton against it, and neither has ever beaten the other for good.

sources.section: III. The Kingdom Behind the Throne, 4A 1000 to 4A 1729

paragraphs.text: The Dark Lands lie between the North Lands and the Middle Lands, and much of them belongs to nobody. Bordon, Dreson, Dulundur, the Troll Forest and a dozen orc and goblin holds answer only to themselves. Smash, a troll king, and the hobgoblin king rule their own realms, not every troll or goblin, and not every monster of the Dark Lands serves Volgan, although his envoys court them all.
paragraphs.note: The independent realms and kings are established; Volgan’s envoys courting them is proposed.

plate.subject: a lone figure climbing out of a chasm, back turned

paragraphs.text: In the Fourth Age Afrit sought the greatest surviving artifacts of Aoaz, and above all he coveted the Necklace of the Abyss. It was held in the depths of the Ember Lands by Roka, a huge being of the rhinoceros-headed people of the Abyss. No chronicle tells the true history of that people or how the necklace was made.

sources.section: II. Roka's necklace and the gathering of powers

paragraphs.text: Rather than enter the Abyss himself, Afrit sent a master thief, Sevrin the Unending, and promised him eternal life if he brought the necklace back. Sevrin crossed hostile lands, reached Roka’s domain and took the artifact by means that are not known. He returned in 4A 1611, and Afrit kept the bargain, using the necklace’s magic to grant him unending life.
paragraphs.note: The thief, the mission and the gift of eternal life are established; the name Sevrin and the year are proposed.

sources.section: II. Roka's necklace and the gathering of powers
III. The Kingdom Behind the Throne, 4A 1000 to 4A 1729

paragraphs.text: The gift had a price. Sevrin ceased to age, but he can still suffer pain, capture and injury, and because his life hangs on Afrit’s hold over the necklace, the thief who was promised freedom from death became a servant who cannot leave.

sources.section: II. Roka's necklace and the gathering of powers

paragraphs.text: The necklace greatly increased the power that Afrit could draw and direct, and it was at its strongest in Aenor, where centuries of worship had prepared his principal seat. Between 4A 1611 and 4A 1700 he gathered lesser artifacts through trade, theft, excavation and bargains with servants across Aoaz: the Ring of Doors, the Crown of Witnesses and the Bracelet of the First Seal.
paragraphs.note: The necklace’s power and the gathering of further artifacts are established; the names of the lesser artifacts and the dates are proposed.

sources.section: II. Roka's necklace and the gathering of powers

paragraphs.text: It is not known what became of Roka, or whether he guarded the necklace himself.

In 4A 1702 the Gunwaith–Girdon wars divided the West Lands. Each side courted Aenoran gold, and both resented it. The fighting went on along their border for half a century, and the crowns between the two kingdoms could not stop it alone.

sources.section: III. The Kingdom Behind the Throne, 4A 1000 to 4A 1729

paragraphs.text: In 4A 1745 Gunwaith and Girdon signed the Truce of the Grey Ford, and the West Lands were quiet for the first time in a generation. In 4A 1748 the truce holds, though uneasily.

Two dozen kingdoms crowd the West Lands. Kradlon, Corogon, Varnondor, Lambin and the Buldor companies trade with Aenor across the wide central sea and resent its tariffs, and every western court remembers that Aenor once tried to rule them. For now the West Lands are divided and at peace.
paragraphs.note: The West Lands’ memory of Aenor’s First Age conquests is established; the trade and tariffs are proposed.

paragraphs.text: The Truce of the Grey Ford is broken. Gunwaith and Girdon took up their old quarrel at the ford, and the West Lands were at war with themselves again.

sources.section: V. The end of the age, 4A 1748 to 4A 1760

paragraphs.text: In 4A 1716 Lerendor’s envoys came to Parim over a disputed toll and were humiliated before the court. The toll was a small matter and the insult was not, so the Leren court began to doubt the Treaty of the Narrow Strait, under which the North Lands must defend Aenor in war.

sources.section: III. The Kingdom Behind the Throne, 4A 1000 to 4A 1729

paragraphs.text: The Leren court has resented Aenor ever since. In Sonargur men ask what an old alliance is worth when its partner in Parim treats Leren envoys like toll-clerks, and the question is put over wine more often than the Treaty is toasted.
The quarrel became a breach. Lerendor withdrew from the Treaty of the Narrow Strait, and the old alliance of the North no longer bound the Leren crown to Aenor’s defence.

sources.section: V. The end of the age, 4A 1748 to 4A 1760

plate.subject: gilded halls, office-buyers queuing at a door

paragraphs.text: The Golden King was crowned in 4A 1729 and sold offices within the year. He is greedy, extravagant and deeply concerned with his own grandeur: he hoards treasure, sells offices and favours those who flatter him. No chronicle gives his own name, and Aenor knows him only as the Golden King.
paragraphs.note: The Golden King’s character and his sale of offices are established; the year of his crowning is proposed.

sources.section: III. The Golden King and the empty throne

paragraphs.text: In 4A 1733 the Golden Court was completed in Parim, a palace district of gilded halls where offices, titles and charters are bought. The dominions whose taxes pay for the gilding grumble at it.

Aenor still works, because the courts, temples and offices that earlier generations built are strong, and the kingdom the Golden King inherited was flourishing. In 4A 1748 he is in the nineteenth year of his reign, and the wits of Parim say that his worst crime is his taste in gold leaf.
paragraphs.note: The strong inherited kingdom is established; the length of the reign and the jest are proposed.

paragraphs.text: In 4A 1741 he founded the Lost Cause, a league against the powers of the dark, named himself its first lord and spent its first treasury on a triumph.
paragraphs.note: The founding of the Lost Cause is established; the year and the triumph are proposed.

paragraphs.text: In 4A 1736 a Mirolonese envoy warned Parim that the Ember Lands were arming. The court laughed, because Volgan had been quiet for longer than Aenor had had kings.

Mirolon, the human kingdom that Volgan conquered in the First Age, is free again and stands in his way, and its scouts still watch the passes and count the dust on the southern roads. Nobody outside Mirolon takes their reports seriously, and the courts of the north think Volgan a spent legend.
paragraphs.note: Mirolon as Volgan’s free rival is established; the scouts and the courts’ disbelief are proposed.

paragraphs.text: In 4A 1744 island fishermen told of black ships among the islands of the Kusmeel, the grave-sea north of Zol’s Mistake. Nobody in a royal court believed them. The fishermen tell it still, and some of them will not put in at a black island for any price.

In 4A 1746 Afrit’s Hidden Council met in secret and concluded that the Golden King had become a liability. The dominions grumbled at his taxes, and the Lost Cause he had founded could become a rival centre of power in the hands of anyone who took it seriously.

Afrit decided that the time had come to stop ruling through human kings. Preparations for the King’s death began, known only to the Council, and its design was to make the succession a crisis that no ordinary claimant could settle, so that the temples could proclaim Aurevan the one protector whose blessing had preserved the kingdom for centuries.
paragraphs.note: Afrit’s decision to take the throne and to arrange the King’s death is established; the Council’s meeting of 4A 1746 and the name Aurevan are proposed.

sources.section: III. The Golden King and the empty throne

paragraphs.text: Outside the Council nobody knows. In 4A 1748 the Golden King still feasts in his gilded halls, the temples still bless him, and the Council’s servants still carry out his orders as faithfully as they ever did.

plate.subject: Parim at dawn over the Great Lake

paragraphs.text: On 1 Lumae 4A 1748 Aoaz has known peace for more than seventeen centuries, and almost nobody alive remembers a war that threatened everyone at once. Nobody is at war with anybody who matters. The borders are quiet, trade flows and the temples are full, and the Golden King, in the nineteenth year of his reign, is thought to have no worse fault than his taste in gold leaf.

Some three hundred crowns, dominions, clans and island lordships divide the continent. The great powers are Aenor and its Concord in the Middle Lands, Lerendor in the North Lands, Coldor in the Cold Lands, Noris and Stabilo in the East Lands, Goldoroth and Dondor in the Dark Lands, Volgan in the Ember Lands, and Zol’s Mistake in the black north.

In the Magical Lands the elves keep their old separation behind the Great Wall, and pilgrims climb to the Worshipdom in the Zilin Hills. In the Cold Lands, the largest and least known land of Aoaz, tribes, yeti, giants and free towns live by trade, herding and hunting. In the far south-west the Sunhot elves keep their many small realms in peace, and among them the Gala elves keep their ancient court under King Lorien.

The West Lands are divided and at peace under the Truce of the Grey Ford. The island lordships fish and chart and now and then rob one another, the East Lands count their caravan money, and the Islands of the South are small, poor and hospitable. In Parim the scholars who keep these histories have little to write beyond the ordinary quarrels of courts.
